assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED made strong, controllable light-matter coupling available on a chip: dispersive readout, microwave resonators as buses and the architecture underlying essentially every superconducting processor. The idea is original, clean and has had very broad impact, from quantum optics to quantum computing. From my own subject area I find it close to decisive for the field.
assessment.attribution: Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin, Schoelkopf wrote the 2004 proposal and the Wallraff-Schoelkopf experiment demonstrated strong coupling the same year; a three-person prize with Blais (theory) and Wallraff and Schoelkopf (experiment) is a natural configuration. Other contributors (Huang, Girvin, Majer, Devoret's group) are not in the supplied credit and I cannot extend it.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by many independent groups over two decades and now industrially deployed. Timeliness is delicate because the 2025 prize recognised macroscopic quantum effects in superconducting circuits; a further superconducting-circuit award may look premature or repetitive to the committee, and I have connections to this community that I would disclose.
uncertainties: Risk of back-to-back recognition of superconducting circuits after 2025.
I have not independently verified the exact credit split between theory and experiment.
Whether the committee would prefer a different framing, such as quantum error correction.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock, with the magic-wavelength idea, gives fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 and opens relativistic geodesy, tests of fundamental constants and a path to redefining the second. The concept is original and clean, with decisive measurable impact.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and first realised strontium lattice clocks; Ye's group drove the accuracy and stability to record levels. Both names are credited and form a sensible two-person prize. Others (e.g. Hall, Lemonde, Takamoto) may need consideration, but I can only choose from the supplied names.
assessment.maturity: Many independent laboratories reproduce and compare clocks, and the results are stable. Recognition seems timely and mature, though the redefinition of the second has not yet occurred.
uncertainties: Whether the 2005 prize for optical frequency combs reduces room for a further precision-measurement award.
Credit for early lattice-clock work by others is not captured in the supplied names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum error correction shows that quantum information can be protected in principle, and with the threshold theorem that large computation is possible. It is conceptually profound and is the central requirement for useful quantum computers, which matters greatly to my field.
assessment.attribution: Shor's nine-qubit code and Steane's CSS-type codes are foundational; Kitaev's toric code and fault-tolerance ideas are decisive in a different direction. The credited trio can cover this, but Gottesman, Calderbank, Knill, Laflamme, Preskill and others contributed centrally, so the allocation is contested and a three-person limit forces unfair exclusions.
assessment.maturity: Experimental demonstrations of below-threshold logical qubits in superconducting, ion and neutral-atom platforms are recent and still early; the field has not delivered fault-tolerant machines. The theory is mature, the experiments are arguably premature for a physics prize.
uncertainties: Large number of deserving contributors makes a fair three-person configuration hard.
Unclear whether the committee would view this as physics or computer science.
Experimental maturity is still developing.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal for ion-trap quantum gates and its experimental realisation gave the first controllable platform for quantum computation, with lasting influence on gate protocols, entanglement and quantum simulation. The scientific impact is high and clear.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller proposed the gate; Blatt realised the gate, deterministic entanglement and long-lived processors. Wineland's prize in 2012 covered ion manipulation, which interacts with the credit story. Credit for the Cirac-Zoller pair also appears in other candidates (B014, B027), so I treat them as one combined body of work.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed across many groups and now a commercial platform. Timing is reasonable; 2012 recognised Wineland and Haroche so some may regard this area as partly honoured.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 prize and with other Cirac-Zoller candidates.
Whether Wineland's and others' contributions make the three-person set incomplete.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 topological insulator opened a whole class of topological band phases with protected edge and surface states. The idea is original and has had very broad impact across condensed-matter physics.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the decisive theoretical proposal; Molenkamp's group gave the first experimental realisation in HgTe wells following Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang. Bernevig, Zhang, Hughes, Fu and others are not included, so this is a contested allocation.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed by many experiments (ARPES, transport) and clearly mature. Recognition is timely and possibly overdue, though the 2016 prize touched topology.
uncertainties: Many contributors (Zhang, Bernevig, Moore, Balents, Fu, Hasan) are outside the supplied names.
Partial overlap with the 2016 prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene opened moire quantum materials, with correlated insulators and superconductivity at a tunable flat band, and created a new field. The theory prediction followed by experiment is a strong narrative of originality.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted the flat band at the magic angle; Jarillo-Herrero's group observed the correlated and superconducting states. A natural three-person set, though other experimental groups (Dean, Young, Yazdani and others) also contributed.
assessment.maturity: Roughly seven years since the discovery; many groups confirm the phenomena, but microscopic mechanisms, e.g. the origin of superconductivity, remain debated. It may be slightly early.
uncertainties: Mechanism of superconductivity not settled.
Sample-dependence and reproducibility concerns in the early years.
Other experimental credit not captured.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Semiconductor quantum-dot spin qubits link mesoscopic physics to quantum computing, from the Loss-DiVincenzo proposal to coherent control, two-qubit gates and silicon implementations. This is close to my own background, which means I should be cautious about favouring it. Scientifically it is significant but is less foundational than circuit QED or error correction.
assessment.attribution: Loss proposed the concept; Tarucha and Vandersypen realised single-spin control and multi-qubit devices. DiVincenzo's co-credit is absent from this entry, and Kouwenhoven, Marcus, Petta and Yacoby also contributed.
assessment.maturity: Rapidly maturing with high-fidelity silicon gates, but scalable systems are not yet established, so the field may be too young for a prize.
uncertainties: Credit split is contested and DiVincenzo is not in the supplied names.
Scalability is unproven.
Possible bias from familiarity with the field.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum control of mechanical motion demonstrated ground-state cooling, quantum states of macroscopic oscillators and entanglement with light or circuits. It extends the macroscopic quantum theme and has uses in sensing and transduction. The impact is meaningful but narrower than the others on my list.
assessment.attribution: Cleland demonstrated a mechanical resonator in the quantum ground state with a superconducting qubit; Aspelmeyer and Kippenberg developed cavity optomechanics and cooling. O'Connell, Teufel, Lehnert, Painter and others are not credited here, so allocation is uncertain.
assessment.maturity: Experimentally well confirmed, but practical impact is still developing and the topic may be seen as an extension of the 2025 prize.
uncertainties: Overlap in theme with the 2025 prize.
Credit allocation among many groups is unresolved.
Long-term impact is less certain.
